claims.text: A dense Cr2O3-rich passive film is a primary cause of enhanced corrosion resistance in chromium-rich steels.
The Cr2O3-rich passive film is stable and self-healing.
Grain refinement produces a higher grain-boundary density that accelerates chromium transport to damaged surface regions.
Controlled minor alloying can optimize chromium availability at the steel surface.
Increased grain-boundary area supports faster formation and repair of a Cr2O3 passive layer.
A dense Cr2O3-rich film acts as a barrier to corrosive species and reduces dissolution of the underlying metal.
The passive film may act as a redox buffer in aggressive media and thereby lower local corrosion kinetics.
Fine-grained, microstructure-engineered steels will have lower corrosion current densities than coarse-grained steels.
Fine-grained, microstructure-engineered steels will undergo slower passive-film breakdown than coarse-grained steels.
Fine-grained, microstructure-engineered steels will show less corrosion penetration than coarse-grained steels.
Grain-refined steels will form a thicker and more uniform Cr2O3-rich surface layer than coarse-grained steels.
Conventional coarse-grained high-chromium stainless or duplex steels display passivation behavior.
The proposed mechanism requires chromium content above a passivation threshold that is typically about 12–15 wt.% Cr.
The mechanism applies only under environmental conditions that permit oxide-film formation and stability.
Extreme irradiation or mechanical damage may alter chromium diffusion kinetics and passivation behavior.
Interactions with other alloying elements may modify the corrosion response of multicomponent steels.

Failure of the refined steel to improve corrosion current, Cr2O3-layer characteristics, or penetration depth relative to the composition-matched coarse-grained control would falsify the proposed grain-boundary-mediated mechanism.
